name: Cianidanol ((+)-cyanidanol-3, a flavonoid tested as a liver drug)
short: Case reports: severe immune haemolytic anaemia, low platelets, kidney failure (title only). 1984 study: liver worse in two thirds with chronic active hepatitis. Trials: fever, haemolysis, hives.
text: Cianidanol ((+)-cyanidanol-3) is a flavonoid that was tested as a drug for liver disease; its most serious reported harm is severe immune haemolysis, the destruction of red blood cells by antibodies. In a 1987 report of six patients who developed haemolysis while receiving the drug (the abstract does not say what they were treated for), the episodes resolved after it was stopped; the causative antibodies could still be shown in all six, even when the episode was more than a year earlier, and two had developed antibodies against their own red cells (autoantibodies). A 1987 series of 5 cases of autoimmune haemolysis reported rapid remission within 2.5 to 10 weeks of stopping it, and its authors state that long-term treatment may induce IgG autoantibodies against red cells with or without overt haemolysis. In a 1992 report, 3 of 5 patients who received cianidanol for 4 to 36 months developed both haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia (low platelets) and 2 had thrombocytopenia alone; blood counts returned to normal in all after it was stopped. Single case reports describe acute haemolytic anaemia in a 36-year-old with chronic active hepatitis 2 weeks after a second course, several episodes of acute intravascular immune haemolysis in a 68-year-old, and repeated severe episodes in a 75-year-old woman with chronic active hepatitis whose antibodies were still present 4 years later; in two reports the patients' antibodies also reacted with rutin, another flavonoid. A 1987 letter with no abstract is titled as describing acute renal failure (kidney failure) due to cianidanol-induced haemolytic anaemia. On the other side, a 1983 report of three patients with liver cirrhosis and hepatitis and immune haemolytic anaemia found no antibodies against the drug, so a causal link could not be proved. In the two placebo-controlled trials cited here, fever was the side effect reported most often. In a 1986 placebo-controlled trial in 338 patients with chronic hepatitis B (174 given cianidanol for 16 weeks), the drug was described as well tolerated, the only notable side effect being a transient fever reaction in 13 patients. In a 1985 controlled trial in 40 patients with chronic active hepatitis (22 given cianidanol), side effects were fever in four, haemolysis in one and urticaria (hives) in one, all subsiding when it was stopped. In a 1984 study of cianidanol given alone to 18 people with alcoholic liver disease and 12 with chronic active hepatitis, most complaints lessened or stopped in both groups and liver histology improved in most of those with alcoholic liver injury, but it worsened in two thirds of those with chronic active hepatitis, whose ALT (SGPT) and alkaline phosphatase levels rose; the abstract describes no control group. In a 1986 comparative study in which 57 people with chronic liver disease took cianidanol tablets for 3 months, dyspeptic side effects led 2 to stop the drug. A 1988 study of 12 men given it with interferon reported minimal side effects, and a 1988 laboratory study refers to a variety of reports of adverse reactions, especially haemolytic anaemia and drug fever. Interactions: in 8 patients with chronic alcoholic hepatitis, cianidanol taken by mouth lowered the clearance of antipyrine (a test drug) and other markers of liver drug metabolism, while the handling of sulphadimidine (another test drug) was not remarkably changed; the authors concluded that it inhibits the liver enzymes that break down medicines. The abstract reports no clinical effects on other medicines.
